list-item.p: Upregulation of Bmpr2 was identified as a central cause of glomerular endothelial cell activation and injury in lupus nephritis.
Glomerular endothelial cells with elevated Bmpr2 expression promoted inflammatory differentiation of macrophages.
C5a mediated the increase in Bmpr2 expression in glomerular endothelial cells.

sec.title: Background
sec.p: Lupus nephritis, a severe complication of SLE, is closely associated with the abnormal activation of glomerular endothelial cells. Despite its significance, the core mechanisms underlying glomerular endothelial cell activation remain elusive.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: We performed single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) on kidney tissues from lupus nephritis patients and mouse models to investigate transcriptional alterations in glomerular endothelial cells and validated our findings in two lupus nephritis models: pristane-induced lupus nephritis and murphy roths large/lpr mice. Genetically modified mice and cultured cells were used to further validate the key discoveries.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Bmpr2 was identified as a critical regulator, showing significant upregulation in glomerular endothelial cells from both lupus nephritis patients and mouse models. Elevated Bmpr2 expression correlated with enhanced glomerular endothelial cell proliferation and migration and increased expression of adhesion molecules (Vcam1, Icam1). BMPR2 activated SMA- and MAD-related proteins-dependent pathways, leading to the upregulation of downstream targets ID1 and ID3, thereby promoting glomerular endothelial cell hyperactivation. Bmpr2 overexpression amplified glomerular endothelial cell proliferation and migration, whereas inhibition of inhibitor of DNA binding signaling by 4-[6-[4-[2-(4-Morpholinyl)ethoxy]phenyl]pyrazolo[1,5-a]pyrimidin-3-yl]quinoline (DMH2) or endothelial-specific Bmpr2 knockout attenuated these effects. Moreover, targeting BMPR2 signaling reduced the infiltration of CD86+ macrophages into lupus nephritis kidneys. Coculture experiments confirmed that Bmpr2-activated glomerular endothelial cells promoted macrophage differentiation into an inflammatory phenotype. Complement component C5a was identified as a critical upstream inducer of Bmpr2 in glomerular endothelial cells, and inhibition of C5a signaling with the C5aR1 antagonist PMX-53 effectively suppressed Bmpr2 upregulation.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: These findings highlight BMPR2 as a key regulator of glomerular endothelial cell injury and macrophage-mediated inflammation in lupus nephritis. Targeting BMPR2 or its upstream activators, such as C5a, effectively treated and improved lupus nephritis.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Lupus nephritis, the most common and severe complication of SLE, significantly reduces patients’ quality of life and increases the SLE mortality rate by nearly 80%.1 Within 10 years of being diagnosed with lupus nephritis, 5%–30% of patients progress to kidney failure.2 In addition, the incidence of lupus nephritis is higher in Asia compared with other regions, at both diagnosis and during follow-ups.3 As a typical autoimmune kidney disease, immunomodulatory treatment is central to lupus nephritis management.4 Despite considerable advancements in treatment protocols over the past decade, the prognosis for lupus nephritis has not achieved the desired improvement.5

A wealth of research has established the central immunoregulatory role of endothelial cells in the onset and progression of lupus nephritis.6 Glomerular endothelial cells (GECs) are the first to interact with autoantibodies, immune complexes, and immune cells. Inflammatory cytokines and shear stress induce GEC injury, leading to abnormal activation and proliferation. This promotes cytokine release, immune cell infiltration, and ultimately kidney fibrosis.7–9 Moreover, hyperproliferative GECs contribute to capillary loop obliteration and extracellular matrix deposition, accelerating glomerulosclerosis. The pathologic effects of endothelial cell proliferation and activation extend beyond the kidneys, making glomerular endothelial dysfunction a major factor in the higher mortality associated with lupus nephritis.10 Therefore, preserving glomerular endothelial function is crucial for controlling renal inflammation and improving the prognosis of lupus nephritis.

In this study, we generated lupus nephritis mouse models and assessed endothelial changes using single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq), identifying Bmpr2 as closely associated with abnormal glomerular endothelial proliferation and migration. We conducted both in vivo and in vitro gene editing experiments to investigate the therapeutic potential of targeting BMPR2 in lupus nephritis, as well as the underlying cause of BMPR2 upregulation (Figure 1A).

sec.title: Animals and Cell Culture
sec.p: All mice were obtained from Cygen Biotechnology Co., Ltd. Lupus nephritis was induced in 8-week-old female BALB/c mice using a single intraperitoneal injection of 500 µl Pristane (Aladdin, P106824), while control mice received saline. Murphy roths large (MRL)/mouse, P strain, Jackson Laboratory (MpJ)-Faslpr (MRL/lpr) mice developed disease spontaneously, and MRL/MpJ mice serve as controls. Endothelial-specific Bmpr2 knockout mice were generated by crossing Bmpr2flox/flox mice with Cdh5-Cre transgenic mice. In accordance with the Animal Research: Reporting of In Vivo Experiments guidelines, we selected a sample size of five mice per group. This number was chosen to balance statistical power with ethical considerations, minimizing animal usage while ensuring reliable and accurate results. All mice used in this study were female. Lupus nephritis predominantly affects females, and female mice are generally considered to develop the disease more typically in animal models. Primary mouse GECs (Meisen, CTCC-U003-MIC) were cultured in DMEM (Gibco, C11995500BT) supplemented with 10% FBS (ExCell, FSP500) and 1% penicillin-streptomycin (Hyclone, SV30010).

Details of the animal and cell experiments, including the administration protocols for the inhibitor of DNA binding (ID) inhibitor 4-[6-[4-[2-(4-Morpholinyl)ethoxy]phenyl]pyrazolo[1,5-a]pyrimidin-3-yl]quinoline (DMH2) (MCE, HY-110245) and C5a antagonist PMX53 (MCE, HY-106178), can be found in the Supplemental Methods and Supplemental Table 6.

sec.title: Human Participants and Clinical Data
sec.p: Kidney biopsy tissues from three lupus nephritis patients diagnosed in 2022–2023 at Sir Run Run Shaw Hospital, Zhejiang University School of Medicine, were selected for snRNA-seq. Lupus nephritis was diagnosed based on the International Society of Nephrology/Renal Pathology Society classification criteria. Inclusion criteria included pathologic and clinical indicators consistent with Class 3 or 4 lupus nephritis and an eGFR >90 ml/min per 1.73 m2. Adjacent healthy kidney tissues from three nephrectomy patients with renal cell carcinoma at the same hospital served as controls, all with eGFR >90 ml/min per 1.73 m2.

sec.title: Statistical Analyses
sec.p: Detailed procedures for kidney single-nucleus isolation, snRNA-seq, and data analysis are provided in the Supplemental Methods.11 Statistical analyses were performed using R software. Unpaired two-tailed t tests were used for two-group comparisons and ANOVA for multiple groups, and Tukey's Honestly Significant Difference was used for post hoc comparisons. Data are presented as mean±SEM, with significance set at P < 0.05. Bar graphs were generated using GraphPad Prism (Version 9.5).

sec.title: Single-Nucleus RNA Sequencing Identified Endothelial Cells in Murine Kidneys
sec.p: We established lupus nephritis mouse models using two approaches: pristane injection and the spontaneous MRL/lpr model. To minimize confounding effects from Fas mutations, sequencing and analyses were conducted mainly on pristane-induced mice. Lupus nephritis mice were divided into two groups and euthanized at 3 and 6 months postpristane injection to represent different disease stages. Mice injected with saline served as controls. Hematoxylin and eosin staining and periodic acid–Schiff (PAS)–stained kidney sections (Supplemental Figure 1, A and B, and Supplemental Table 1) revealed significant GEC proliferation at 3 months, with inflammatory cell infiltration and partial capillary occlusion. By 6 months, these changes progressed to near-complete capillary occlusion and glomerulosclerosis, while control kidneys showed minimal pathology (Figure 1B).

We then assessed IgG and C3 deposition in the kidneys. At 3 months, significant deposits were observed (Figure 1C), with IgG and C3 deposition at 10% and 12%, respectively (Supplemental Figure 1, C and D). By 6 months, these deposits increased to 23% and 22%. The urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) at 3 months was 80 µg/mg, more than double the control level, and increased to 200 µg/mg by 6 months (Figure 1D). Anti-dsDNA levels in the serum were also elevated, reaching 32 international unit/ml at 3 months and 45 international unit/ml at 6 months (Figure 1E). These findings confirm successful establishment of lupus nephritis models at varying severities.

Next, we randomly selected three mice from each group for snRNA-seq. After strict quality control, 92,326 high-quality nuclei were obtained from nine kidney samples. After optimal dimensionality reduction (Supplemental Figure 2, A and B), two clusters with high expression of endothelial markers Flt1 and Ptprb were identified.12 The remaining 13 kidney cell types were categorized based on markers identified in previous studies (Figure 1, F and G).13

Notably, the marker gene for the distal convoluted tubule, Slc12a3,14 and the marker for collecting tubules, Slc8a1,15 were coexpressed in the same cluster (Supplemental Figure 2D), labeled as distal convoluted tubule or connecting tubule. We also observed diversity in the thick ascending limb cell population, including a subset with elevated Nos1 (macula densa) and Atp10b expression (thin ascending limb) (Supplemental Figure 2E).13,16 In addition, Upk3a,17 a marker for urothelial cells, was highly expressed in one of the clusters. The proportion of endothelial cells in early-stage lupus nephritis mice was similar to controls but nearly three-fold higher in late-stage mice (Figure 1H and Supplemental Figure 2F).

Enrichment analysis of differentially expressed genes in endothelial cells showed that control endothelial cells were highly active in kidney development (Supplemental Figure 2G). In 3M-lupus nephritis mice, endothelial cells exhibited enhanced activity in cell proliferation and migration pathways (Supplemental Figure 2H), while at 6 months, there was increased activity in cell adhesion and T-cell activation, indicating functional transitions in endothelial cells across disease stages (Supplemental Figure 2I).

Finally, 8888 endothelial cells were subjected to dimensionality reduction and reclustering. Based on previous studies, these cells were classified into vascular progenitors, vasa recta, peritubular capillaries, and GECs (Figure 1, I and J),18 with the highest glomerular endothelial density observed in 6M-lupus nephritis mice (Figure 1K). Enrichment analysis revealed that high-expression genes in GECs from 3M-lupus nephritis mice were associated with migration, while 6M-lupus nephritis were enriched for both proliferation and migration (Figure 1, L–N).

sec.title: Significant Alterations in Proliferation and Migration Activity of GEC in Lupus Nephritis
sec.p: After inflammation and injury, endothelial cells undergo changes in activity, including proliferation, differentiation, migration, and adhesion. Based on enrichment analysis,19 we focused on changes in proliferation and migration activities during endothelial repair in lupus nephritis (Supplemental Table 2). Compared with controls, endothelial cells from lupus nephritis mice showed significant increases in both proliferation and migration, particularly in the early stages (Figure 2A). Two-dimensional visualization revealed that endothelial cells with higher activity were mainly clustered in regions occupied by GEC (Figure 2B). Among endothelial subtypes, the most notable changes in activity were observed in GEC, with moderate increases in peritubular capillaries and vasa recta cells compared with controls (Figure 2C).

sec.p: To validate this finding, we collected kidney biopsy samples from three female lupus nephritis patients, aged 20–50 years, with systemic lupus erythematosus disease activity index scores between 6 and 12, for snRNA-seq. All patients had normal kidney function and had not used immunosuppressants or steroids before the biopsy. Detailed clinical parameters are presented in Supplemental Table 3.

Following the same principles (Supplemental Figure 3A), we used commonly employed cell markers to classify the cells from human kidneys into 11 cell types including endothelial cells (Figure 2, D and E).20 Compared with controls, the proportion of endothelial cells in lupus nephritis was reduced (Figure 2F). However, we also note that this observation may be attributed to the disproportionately low capture of endothelial cells in kidney samples from some lupus nephritis patients (Supplemental Figure 3B). Similarly, the 1794 endothelial cells identified from human kidneys were reclustered into three types: GECs, peritubular capillaries, and afferent/efferent arterioles (Figure 2, G and H).21 Peritubular capillaries were the most prevalent endothelial subtype, while the proportion of GECs remained lower in lupus nephritis patients compared with controls due to sample heterogeneity (Figure 2I and Supplemental Figure 3C). Proliferation activity of endothelial cells in lupus nephritis was significantly increased, while migration activity slightly decreased (Figure 2J). Notably, GECs and afferent/efferent arteriole cells exhibited the highest proliferation and migration activities, whereas peritubular capillaries were relatively decreased, consistent with findings in mice (Figure 2, K and L).

sec.title: Cross-Species Identification of BMPR2 as a Key Regulator of GECs Proliferation and Migration in Lupus Nephritis
sec.p: To clarify the genes driving the increase in glomerular endothelial proliferation and migration, we analyzed upregulated genes in endothelial cells from both lupus nephritis mice and patients (Figure 3A). By intersecting these with proliferation- and migration-related gene sets, we identified BMPR2 as a key gene significantly upregulated in GECs of both human and mice (Figure 3B and Supplemental Table 4). Specifically, eight genes associated with proliferation and migration were upregulated in mouse GECs (Figure 3C), while seven genes were upregulated in human GECs (Figure 3D). Notably, BMPR2 was expressed in over 70% of GECs in both species, with the highest expression observed in endothelial cells among all kidney cell types (Figure 3E). Within endothelial subtypes, BMPR2 expression was particularly elevated in both human and mouse GECs, as well as in mouse vascular progenitors (Figure 3F).

sec.p: Multiplex immunofluorescence analysis revealed significant upregulation of BMPR2 expression in corresponding mouse models, including Pristane-induced and MPL/lpr mice (Figure 3G and Supplemental Figures 3, D and E, and 7F). Immunohistochemical staining of three healthy adjacent nontumor tissues from patients with renal cell carcinoma and five lupus nephritis patients (International Society of Nephrology/Renal Pathology Society Class 3 or 4) showed that BMPR2 expression was significantly elevated in the glomerular endothelial regions of lupus nephritis patients (Figure 3H and Supplemental Figure 3, F and G).

BMPR2 mediates SMAD1 phosphorylation on binding with bone morphogenetic protein (BMP)–related ligands, leading to increased expression of ID1 and ID3.22 In GECs of lupus nephritis patients and mouse models, ID1 and ID3 were significantly upregulated, while SMAD1 expression was reduced (Supplemental Figure 3, H and I).

Western blot (WB) analysis showed significant upregulation of BMPR2, ID1, and ID3 in kidneys of early- and late-stage lupus nephritis mice compared with controls. Although SMAD1 levels remained unchanged, phosphorylated SMAD1 was significantly elevated (Figure 3I and Supplemental Figure 4A). The ratio of phosphorylated SMAD1 to SMAD1 was also higher in lupus nephritis mice, confirming the link between lupus nephritis progression and increased renal expression of ID1, ID3, and enhanced SMAD1 phosphorylation (Supplemental Figure 4B).

Furthermore, quantitative PCR (qPCR) analysis revealed elevated mRNA levels of Bmpr2, Id1, and Id3 in lupus nephritis mice (Figure 3, J–L). Although Bmpr2 levels were stable across different stages of lupus nephritis, Id1 and Id3 mRNA levels were higher in late-stage lupus nephritis mice. In addition, Mki67 and Pcna, proliferation markers,23 were significantly upregulated, with Pcna showing a marked increase in late-stage lupus nephritis mice (Figure 3, M and N). In addition, endothelial activation markers Vcam1 and Icam1 were also elevated, especially in late-stage lupus nephritis (Figure 3, O and P)

sec.title: Pharmacologic Inhibition of BMPR2 Downstream Signaling Ameliorated Glomerular Injury in Lupus Nephritis
sec.p: To ascertain the involvement of BMPR2 and its downstream pathways in lupus nephritis, we treated Pristane-injected mice with the ID inhibitor DMH2, which binds to BMPs and modulates ID1 and ID3 expression24 (Figure 4A). Treatment with DMH2 inhibited endothelial proliferation and significantly ameliorated glomerulosclerosis, particularly in the late-stage lupus nephritis mice (Figure 4B and Supplemental Figure 4, C and D). Moreover, DMH2 treatment resulted in a marked reduction in IgG and C3 deposition in the kidneys (Supplemental Figure 4, E–G). Although the UACR in treated lupus nephritis mice remained higher than in healthy controls, it showed a notable decrease compared with untreated mice (Figure 4C). Although DMH2 did not completely prevent lupus nephritis, it alleviated both pathologic and clinical manifestations.

sec.p: Subsequent WB analysis revealed that DMH2 treatment significantly reduced the expression of ID1 and ID3 in both 3M-lupus and 6M-lupus nephritis mice (Figure 4D and Supplemental Figure 4, H and I). In addition, SMAD1 phosphorylation was markedly decreased (Figure 4E and Supplemental Figure 4, J and K). Interestingly, DMH2 treatment prevented Pristane injection from affecting downstream BMPR2 proteins. qPCR analysis revealed a significant reduction in the mRNA levels of Id1 and Id3 (Figure 4, F and G), as well as cell proliferation markers Mki67 and Pcna (Figure 4, H and I). Furthermore, transcription levels of the endothelial activation markers Vcam1 and Icam1 were also significantly decreased (Figure 4, J and K), indicating that DMH2 effectively suppresses endothelial proliferation and activation.

We then cultured mouse GECs in vitro and engineered them to overexpress Bmpr2 using a lentiviral system, confirmed by qPCR (Supplemental Figure 4L). Transwell assays revealed that Bmpr2+ cells had significantly increased migration versus controls. Although ID inhibitors did not fully block this effect, they significantly reduced the migration enhancement seen in untreated Bmpr2+ cells (Figure 4, L and M). Real-time cell analysis results showed a steady increase in proliferation across four groups, with Bmpr2+ cells displaying the highest levels. However, DMH2 treatment significantly reduced the vitality of Bmpr2+ cells (Figure 4N). Furthermore, qPCR analysis demonstrated that the mRNA levels of Id1, Id3 (Figure 4, O and P), Mki67, Pcna, Vcam1, and Icam1 were significantly elevated in Bmpr2+ cells compared with controls. After DMH2 treatment, these gene expressions decreased significantly in Bmpr2+ cells compared with untreated cells (Figure 4, Q–T); these in vitro findings reaffirm that modulating Bmpr2 function can effectively reduce abnormal activation of GECs.

sec.title: Conditional Knockout of Bmpr2 Inhibited Endothelial Cell Activation and Ameliorated Lupus Nephritis
sec.p: We generated Bmpr2+/− mice using a Cdh5 promoter–driven Cre-loxP recombination system, reducing Bmpr2 expression in endothelial cells while maintaining normal growth and development (Figure 5A). Multiple immunofluorescence analysis confirmed that BMPR2 expression was significantly reduced in GEC of Bmpr2+/− mice (Figure 5B and Supplemental Figure 5, A and B). Histologic analysis showed that, after Pristane injection, Bmpr2+/− and wild-type (WT) mice exhibited glomerular endothelial proliferation, but the extent of proliferation was significantly reduced in Bmpr2+/− mice at both 3 and 6 months. By 6 months, most Bmpr2+/− mice showed moderate glomerulosclerosis (Figure 5C and Supplemental Figure 5, C and D). Bmpr2+/− mice also had significantly less IgG and C3 deposition in the glomeruli (Supplemental Figure 5, E–G). Although UACR was elevated in Bmpr2+/− mice at 3 months compared with controls, the difference was not statistically significant. At 6 months, however, the UACR in Bmpr2+/− mice was more than halved compared with WT mice (Figure 5D), supporting the beneficial effects of targeting BMPR2 in improving lupus nephritis.

sec.p: WB analysis indicated that, compared with WT mice, BMPR2 protein levels were significantly decreased in the kidney tissue of Bmpr2+/− mice at both 3 and 6 months post lupus nephritis model induction (Figure 5, E and F). Consistent with this, downstream molecules ID1, ID3 (Figure 5, G and H), and SMA- and MAD-related proteins (SMAD) phosphorylation followed similar trends (Figure 5I). Then, qPCR analysis reveals that Bmpr2+/− mice had significantly lower Bmpr2 mRNA levels compared with controls, with a marked increase in Bmpr2 transcription only after 6 months (Figure 5J), which was accompanied by similar changes in Id1 mRNA levels (Figure 5K). Furthermore, Id3 transcription was also induced by Pristane injection in Bmpr2+/− mice but at significantly lower levels than in WT mice (Figure 5L). The mRNA levels of proliferation markers Mki67 and Pcna (Figure 5, M and N) and endothelial activation markers Vcam1 and Icam1 (Figure 5, O and P) showed a similar pattern, confirming that targeting Bmpr2 effectively inhibits endothelial proliferation and activation.

sec.title: Targeting Bmpr2 Reduced CD86+ Macrophage Infiltration in the Kidneys of Lupus Nephritis
sec.p: Despite the limited ability of snRNA-seq to capture immune cells, we identified 1277 immune cells in murine kidneys. Dimensionality reduction and clustering revealed three distinct clusters: one expressing the T-cell marker Cd24724 and two Apobec1-high clusters classified as macrophages.25,26 One macrophage cluster exhibited high CD86 expression, a marker of M1 macrophages linked to activation and inflammation, while the other was enriched in Vegfa, indicative of proangiogenic, tissue-repairing macrophages.27 These were designated as T cell, CD86+ macrophages, and Vegfa+macrophages clusters (Figure 6, A and B). CD86+ macrophages were more abundant in lupus nephritis mice than in controls (Figure 6C). By contrast, only 364 immune cells were captured in human samples, limiting the identification of more detailed cell types.

caption.p: Increased infiltration of CD86+ macrophages in the kidneys of lupus nephritis mice. (A) Bubble plot showing the expression of macrophages marker Apobec1, T-cell marker Cd247, and markers of two macrophages subtypes, Cd86 and Vegf. (B) UMAP plot displaying the two-dimensional distribution of T cells, Cd86+ macrophages, and Vegf+macrophages. (C) Bar chart showing the proportion changes of three immune cell subtypes in control and lupus nephritis mice. (D) Bar graph of biologic process enrichment analysis for the top 100 upregulated genes in Cd86+ macrophages. (E) Bubble plot showing the expression of several proinflammatory genes, including Cx3cr1, Il6ra, Ifnar1, Ifnar2, C1qa, C1qb, and C1qc, across different macrophages subtypes. (F) Multiple immunofluorescence images showing the expression of F4/80 (green) and CD86 (red) in kidney sections from WT and Bmpr2+/− mice. Nuclei are stained with DAPI (blue). The merged images demonstrate the colocalization of F4/80 and CD86 in macrophages. Scale bar, 30 µm. (G) Experimental workflow of GEC and macrophages coculture. (H–I) Scatter plots showing the effect of Bmpr2 overexpression and DMH2 treatment on Mcp-1 and Tnf-α mRNA levels in GEC, normalized to β-actin. Group: A, GEC; B, GEC+DMH2; C, Bmpr2+ GEC; D, Bmpr2+ GEC+DMH2. (J) Effect of conditioned medium from GEC under different treatments on mRNA levels of Cd86, Il-1β, Il-6, Nos1, and Tnf-α in macrophages. Error bars represent SEM (n=6).

sec.p: Enrichment analysis showed that CD86+ macrophages expressed genes involved in B-cell activation and leukocyte migration (Figure 6D), alongside proinflammatory markers including Cx3cr1, Il6ra, Ifnar1/2, and C1qa/b/c (Figure 6E and Supplemental Table 5). Multiple immunofluorescence staining revealed sparse glomerular CD86+ macrophages in controls but increased abundance in lupus nephritis mice, especially at late stages. Both DMH2 treatment and Bmpr2 knockout reduced CD86+ macrophages infiltration (Figure 6F and Supplemental Figure 5H), implicating Bmpr2 in endothelium-mediated macrophages activation.

To confirm this, we assessed Mcp-1 and TNF-α expression in Bmpr2+ GECs, key cytokines in macrophages activation. Bmpr2+ cells showed elevated transcription of both, which was suppressed by DMH2 (Figure 6, G–I). Supernatants from treated GECs were used to stimulate macrophages, which showed the highest levels of Cd86, TNF-α, Il-1β, Il-6, and Nos2. DMH2 pretreatment significantly reduced these responses (Figure 6J). These findings establish Bmpr2-driven endothelial activation as a promoter of inflammatory macrophages polarization, which can be mitigated by targeting BMPR2.

sec.title: Complement-Derived C5a Drove BMPR2 Overexpression in GEC during Lupus Nephritis
sec.p: C5a is a key complement product elevated in lupus nephritis and correlated with disease severity.28 We found that C5a stimulation led to upregulation of Bmpr2 in GECs, exposure to lupus nephritis patient serum also increased Bmpr2 expression, which was reversed by the C5aR1 antagonist PMX-5329 (Figure 7A and Supplemental Figure 6A), implicating C5a in glomerular endothelial activation and injury through Bmpr2 signaling.

caption.p: C5a mediates increased expression of BMPR2 in GEC of lupus nephritis mice and infiltration of CD86+ macrophages. (A) Scatter plot showing the effect of C5a antagonist on Bmpr2 mRNA levels in GEC. (B) Schematic representation of the therapeutic effects of the C5a antagonist PMX-53 in two lupus nephritis mouse models. (C) H&E and PAS staining images showing the effects of PMX-53 on glomerular pathology in WT and Bmpr2+/− mice. Scale bar, 30 µm. Immunofluorescence images (scale bar, 30 µm) show the deposition of IgG and C3. (D) Multiple immunofluorescence images showing the expression of BMPR2 (green), CD31 (red), F4/80 (green), and CD86 (red) in kidneys of two lupus nephritis mouse models and their corresponding controls before and after PMX-53 treatment. Cell nuclei are stained with DAPI (blue). Scale bar, 30 µm. MpJ, mouse, P strain, Jackson Laboratory; MRL, murphy roths large.

sec.p: We next quantified serum C5a in two lupus nephritis mouse models. In BALB/c mice, levels rose from 160 ng/ml at 3 months to 300 ng/ml at 6 months post–Pristane injection, approximately ten-fold higher than controls (Supplemental Figure 6B). In MRL/lpr mice, C5a levels reached 60 ng/ml at 8 weeks and 400 ng/ml after 3 months, exceeding those in MRL/MpJ mice (Supplemental Figure 6C).

To assess whether blocking C5a–C5aR1 signaling mitigates endothelial injury and kidney pathology, both lupus nephritis models were treated with PMX-53 (Figure 7B). After 3 months, both models showed a nearly 50% reduction in UACR (Supplemental Figure 6D), accompanied by decreased glomerular endothelial proliferation, reduced inflammatory infiltration and capillary occlusion, as well as markedly improved IgG and C3 deposition (Figure 7C and Supplemental Figure 6, E–H).

Multiplex immunofluorescence staining revealed that PMX-53 reduced BMPR2 expression, suggesting C5a dependence. In both models, PMX-53 also significantly decreased CD86+ macrophage infiltration in the glomeruli (Figure 7D and Supplemental Figure 6, I–K).

We then treated 3-month-old MRL/lpr mice, which exhibited significant lupus nephritis features (Figure 8A). After 1 month of DMH2 or PMX-53 treatment, we observed significant reductions in UACR (Figure 8B), IgG and C3 deposition, and glomerulosclerosis (Figure 8C). PMX-53 treatment also resulted in marked suppression of BMPR2 in GECs (Supplemental Figure 7, A and B). Furthermore, flow cytometric analysis of endothelial cells from the kidney cortex and glomeruli revealed that PMX-53 treatment significantly inhibited abnormal endothelial proliferation (Figure 8D and Supplemental Figure 7, C and D). These findings support the potential of targeting the BMPR2 axis in lupus nephritis.

caption.p: DMH2 and PMX-53 effectively treat established lupus nephritis mouse models. (A) Schematic diagram illustrating the therapeutic effects of the ID inhibitor DMH2 and the C5a antagonist PMX-53 in MRL/lpr mice with established lupus nephritis phenotype. (B) Scatter plot showing the therapeutic effect of DMH2 and PMX-53 on the UACR in MRL/lpr mice with established lupus nephritis phenotype. (C) H&E and PAS staining images showing the effects of PMX-53 on glomerular pathology in WT and Bmpr2+/− mice. Scale bar, 30 µm. Immunofluorescence images (scale bar, 30 µm) show the deposition of IgG and C3. In addition, the scatter plots display endothelial cell proliferation, glomerulosclerosis scores, and the percentage area of IgG and C3 deposition. (D) Flow cytometry analysis of the percentage of CD31-positive cells in the kidney cortex and isolated glomeruli of mice. CD31+ cells were gated as live, single, CD31+ events. (E) The expression of BMPR2 increases under the stimulation of inflammatory mediators such as C5a, leading to increased phosphorylation of downstream SMAD1, which in turn promotes the expression of ID1 and ID3. This ultimately results in excessive proliferation and activation of GEC and promotes the infiltration of CD86+ macrophages in the kidneys. FCM, flow cytometry.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this study, we find that both in vitro and in vivo experiments demonstrated that Bmpr2 is a key gene mediating these glomerular endothelial functional changes and is associated with the activation of macrophages in lupus nephritis, providing a novel therapeutic target for the prevention and treatment of lupus nephritis (Figure 8E).

Enrichment analysis of endothelial cells in 6-month lupus nephritis mice revealed pathways linked to T-cell activation and adhesion, suggesting that endothelial injury may activate memory T-cell homing, accelerating lupus nephritis progression.30 After glomerular endothelial injury, a series of repair processes are triggered, leading to abnormal activation, secretion of adhesion molecules, and upregulation of proliferation markers. This enhances endothelial proliferation and migration, contributing to glomerular damage and sclerosis.6 Therefore, we initially assessed overall endothelial function and found a marked increase in proliferation and migration in lupus nephritis mice, with GEC exhibiting the highest activity among all subtypes. These changes were primarily driven by the glomerular endothelium and were evident as early as in 3-month-old lupus nephritis mice, indicating a strong reparative response to inflammation-induced injury. Similarly, three early-stage lupus nephritis patients showed significantly increased glomerular endothelial proliferation, consistent with the murine findings. Notably, excessive proliferation of GECs may contribute to glomerulosclerosis and severe kidney impairment.31

Differentially expressed gene analysis identified a significant upregulation of BMPR2 in GECs from both human and Pristane-induced lupus nephritis mouse models. BMPR2, a key member of the BMP receptor family, forms a complex with BMP ligands to regulate downstream gene expression, ultimately controlling cell growth, differentiation, and apoptosis. It plays a role in the pathogenesis of pulmonary hypertension, a common pulmonary complication in SLE.32 Previous studies have shown that BMPR2 signaling activation can reduce apoptosis in pulmonary arterial endothelial cells and enhance endothelial repair.33

However, its involvement in lupus nephritis–associated kidney injury remains unclear. In both human and mouse endothelial subtypes, BMPR2 is primarily expressed in GECs in both humans and mice. We propose that overexpression of BMPR2 in these cells may be a key feature of lupus nephritis, driving glomerular endothelial proliferation and glomerulosclerosis. BMPR2 enhances endothelial activity by activating the SMAD-dependent canonical pathway, promoting ID1 and ID3 transcription,34 and finally drives endothelial proliferation and differentiation, maintaining capillary homeostasis, which is essential for endothelial repair after injury.35 However, excessive BMP signaling activation can cause uncontrolled endothelial growth, contributing to chronic inflammation.36 Studies in CKD have shown that abnormal BMP signaling activation can also result in endothelial dysfunction and injury,37 therefore, maintaining a balance in BMP signaling within endothelial cells may be crucial for the treatment of lupus nephritis.

Multiple immunofluorescence staining, along with WB and qPCR analyses, confirmed the significant Bmpr2 in GECs and the activation of its downstream pathways in lupus nephritis mice. On competitive binding of the ID inhibitor DMH2 to BMPR2, we observed a marked reduction in SMAD phosphorylation, with decreased expression of ID1 and ID3, leading to improved UACR and pathologic manifestations in lupus nephritis mice. Targeting BMPR2 effectively inhibits endothelial cell activation, reduces the secretion of adhesion molecules, and maintains endothelial barrier stability, thereby decreasing IgG and C3 deposition. Notably, WB and qPCR findings were obtained from kidney tissue homogenates. Although we focused on glomerular endothelial cell changes, the area of the renal interstitial capillary bed is much larger than that of the glomeruli. Sn-RNA seq data also showed significant activation of other endothelial cells, suggesting that BMPR2-mediated inflammation may play a role not only in the glomerulus but also in other renal endothelial cells. In vitro, Bmpr2 overexpression significantly enhanced GEC proliferation and migration, effects that were effectively mitigated by the ID inhibitor. In addition, conditional knockout of Bmpr2 also yielded similar therapeutic benefits in lupus nephritis. Previous studies have focused on the role of SMAD phosphorylation in lupus nephritis but primarily in relation to the TGF-β signaling pathway and its association with tubular injury and renal interstitial fibrosis.38,39 Therefore, targeting BMPR2 may offer a more effective therapeutic approach, and early intervention in BMP signaling can significantly reduce endothelial proliferation, thereby mitigating glomerulosclerosis and kidney fibrosis. BMP pathway modulation could be a promising strategy, with substantial benefits even at early stages of the disease.

We identified two key macrophage subtypes in lupus nephritis mice, with CD86+ macrophages being particularly notable due to their increased proportion in lupus nephritis models. Previous studies have reported elevated CD86+ macrophages in lupus nephritis mice,40 and monoclonal antibodies against CD86 have been shown to effectively ameliorate lupus nephritis.41 CD86 expression is closely associated with M1 macrophages,42 and our enrichment analysis indicates that CD86+ macrophages in lupus nephritis mice are involved in proinflammatory pathways, with significant expression of Cx3cr1 and Il6ra, which are related to macrophage migration and activation.43,44 Moreover, IFN receptors were prominently expressed on CD86+ macrophages. In lupus nephritis patients, elevated IFN levels have been linked to enhanced macrophage activation and infiltration in the kidneys, correlating with disease progression and severity.45 We also observed increased expression of C1 complex–related genes in CD86+ macrophages, which plays a dual role in lupus nephritis, contributing to kidney damage while also participating in the clearance of immune complexes and apoptotic cells.46,47 In lupus nephritis mice, CD86+ macrophages may modulate renal inflammation through C1q secretion, and alterations in their function and number are associated with exacerbated kidney damage. Notably, administration of ID inhibitors or Bmpr2 knockout in lupus nephritis mice significantly reduced CD86+ macrophage infiltration into the kidneys. In addition, in vitro analysis of GEC-conditioned medium revealed that supernatants from Bmpr2+ GEC promoted expression of M1 macrophage markers. However, treatment with DMH2 significantly inhibited this effect, indicating that targeting BMPR2 not only inhibits endothelial cell proliferation and activation but also reduces inflammatory macrophage infiltration, ultimately improving lupus nephritis outcomes and slowing disease progression.

Interestingly, C5a significantly increases BMPR2 expression in GEC in vitro. After immune complex deposition in the glomerulus, C1q binds and activates the classical complement pathway, ultimately cleaving C5 to produce large amounts of C5a. This, in turn, recruits neutrophils and monocytes to the glomerulus, further exacerbating inflammation and amplifying complement activation.48 In addition, C5a activates GECs and induces damage through its binding to the C5aR1. This activation promotes the secretion of adhesion molecules, enhancing the adhesion between GECs and immune cells, thereby exacerbating inflammatory damage. Furthermore, C5a forms the membrane attack complex, compromising GECs' integrity and further promoting the release of proinflammatory cytokines. Therefore, C5aR antagonism, by inhibiting the binding of C5a to its receptor, protects endothelial barrier integrity and suppresses the C5a-induced inflammatory cascade. This not only reduces local complement activation but also diminishes the deposition of immune complexes. Although C5aR blockade does not directly impact the generation of upstream complement components, it effectively mitigates the downstream effects of complement activation, thereby alleviating tissue damage.49

The C5aR1 antagonist PMX-53 significantly alleviated glomerular damage and CD86+ macrophage infiltration in both lupus nephritis mouse models, while also inhibiting BMPR2 upregulation. Previous studies have shown that C5a antagonism can reduce endothelial cell and podocyte damage in SLE patients,28,50 and C5a antagonists have demonstrated significant efficacy in vasculitis treatment.51 Furthermore, in established lupus nephritis models, both DMH2 and C5aR1 showed promising therapeutic effects. Admittedly, our study has limitations in interpreting the roles and changes of other renal endothelial subtypes in lupus nephritis, which remains an important focus for future research. Nevertheless, current evidence supports the development and application of BMPR2-targeted therapy for lupus nephritis, offering a potentially reliable alternative to corticosteroids.
